answer_text:
Let  

\[
D=a_1-a_n>0.
\]

Since  

\[
a_1\ge a_2\ge \cdots \ge a_n,
\]

every \(a_i\) lies between \(a_n\) and \(a_1\). Hence

\[
\left|a_i-\frac{a_1+a_n}{2}\right|\le \frac{a_1-a_n}{2}=\frac D2
\qquad (i=1,2,\dots,n).
\]

Because \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=0\), we may subtract the constant \(\frac{a_1+a_n}{2}\) from all \(a_i\) without changing the sum:

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i
=
\sum_{i=1}^n \left(a_i-\frac{a_1+a_n}{2}\right)x_i.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\right|
\le
\sum_{i=1}^n 
\left|a_i-\frac{a_1+a_n}{2}\right| |x_i|
\le
\frac{D}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|.
\]

Using \(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|=1\), we get

\[
\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\right|
\le
\frac{D}{2}
=
\frac12(a_1-a_n).
\]

Thus the inequality holds for \(m=\frac12\), and hence for every \(m\ge \frac12\).

It remains to show that no smaller \(m\) works. Take, for example,

\[
x_1=\frac12,\qquad x_n=-\frac12,\qquad x_2=\cdots=x_{n-1}=0.
\]

Then

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|=1.
\]

For any admissible \(a_1,\dots,a_n\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i
=
\frac12 a_1-\frac12 a_n
=
\frac12(a_1-a_n).
\]

So

\[
\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\right|
=
\frac12(a_1-a_n).
\]

If \(m<\frac12\), then

\[
\frac12(a_1-a_n)>m(a_1-a_n),
\]

so the inequality fails. Therefore the smallest possible value of \(m\) is \(\frac12\), and all larger values also work.

Hence the required range is

\[
\boxed{\left[\frac12,\,+\infty\right)}.
\]
